question: Does the requirment under Article 5 of the Delegated Regulation refer to the sharing of information on the underlying data of the Suspicious Activity report (SAR) (e.g. transactions, customer data) without disclosing whether the SAR was filed and sent to the local authorities of the third country?
ground_truth:
Article 45 of Directive (EU) 2015/849 (AMLD) requires obliged entities that are part of a group to implement group-wide policies and procedures. These group-wide anti money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) policies and procedures, include policies and procedures for sharing information within the group for AML/CFT purposes, and are required to be implemented at the level of branches and majority-owned subsidiaries in Member States and third countries.
Sharing information within the group supports effective, ongoing Money Laundering (ML)/Terrorist Financing (TF) risk identification and management at the level of the group. It is also enables competent authorities to effectively supervise the group's compliance with the AMLD’s requirements.
The AMLD creates an expectation that credit institutions and financial institutions, that form part of the same group, disclose to each other that a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) has been submitted, as well as to disclose the accompanying information of that STR and additional information requested by the financial intelligence unit (FIU).
Specifically, Article 45 (8) of the AMLD provides that credit institutions and financial institutions, that are part of a group, are required to share within the group ‘information on suspicions that funds are the proceeds of criminal activity or are related to terrorist financing’ reported to the financial intelligence unit (FIU), unless otherwise instructed by the FIU. Furthermore, Article 39(3) allows for the said sharing of information to take place notwithstanding the prohibition provided for under Article 39(1) of the AMLD.
Such disclosure is not limited to group entities that are based in the EU but possible also between EU entities and their branches and majority owned subsidiaries established in third countries, subject to certain conditions.
Notwithstanding the requirement of Article 45(8) of the AMLD, the conditions set out in Article 39 of the AMLD, and Article 5 of
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/758
, recognise that the sharing of actual STRs among group entities may not always be possible. In those situations, Article 5 of the Delegated Regulation provides that credit institutions and financial institutions have to take steps to mitigate the resulting ML/ TF risk at group level by:
Ensuring that the third country branch or majority-owned subsidiary provides relevant aggregate information to the credit institution's or financial institution's senior management so that it is able to assess the ML/TF risk associated with the operation of the branch or majority-owned subsidiary and the impact this has on the group, such as: (i) the number of suspicious transactions reported within a set period; (ii) aggregated statistical data providing an overview of the circumstances that gave rise to suspicion; and
taking one or more measures set out in Article 8 a-c and g-i of the Delegated Regulation in addition to their standard AML/CFT measures to manage ML/TF risk across the group. The additional measures in Article 8 include steps to ensure that the branch or majority-owned subsidiary shares with the credit institutions or financial institutions ‘information that gave rise to the knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect that money laundering and terrorist financing was being attempted or had occurred, such as facts, transactions, circumstances and documents upon which suspicions are based, including personal information to the extent that this is possible under the third country's law’.

meta.subject_matter: Disclosure of information within the group related to suspicious activity reports (SARs) to the competent authorities

baseline.text: The requirement under Article 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/847, as transposed into national law, specifically addresses the confidentiality of information shared within a banking group regarding Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) filed with third-country authorities. The regulation mandates that a credit institution must not disclose to other group entities the fact that a SAR has been filed or sent to the competent authorities of a third country, nor may it disclose the underlying data contained within that report, such as transaction details or customer information. This dual prohibition ensures that the existence of a report and the substantive evidence supporting it remain confidential within the group structure. Consequently, the requirement explicitly covers both the metadata indicating the filing status and the underlying data itself. If a group entity were to share the specific transactions or customer data associated with a SAR filed in a third country, this would constitute a breach of the confidentiality obligation. The legislative intent is to prevent the leakage of sensitive investigative data that could compromise ongoing investigations or expose the institution to reputational risk. Therefore, the scope of Article 5 is comprehensive, encompassing the entire package of information generated by the SAR process, including both the notification of the filing and the substantive content of the report. Any disclosure of either element to other group members without the explicit consent of the competent authority of the third country would violate the regulatory framework designed to protect the integrity of anti-money laundering efforts abroad.

dpo.text:
The requirement under Article 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/847, as transposed into national law, does not mandate the disclosure of the underlying data contained within a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) to the competent authorities of a third country. Instead, the obligation is strictly limited to the transmission of the SAR itself, which serves as a formal notification of the existence of a suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing. The underlying data, such as specific transaction details or customer identification information, remains protected under the confidentiality provisions of the relevant national implementing measures and the broader framework of Directive (EU) 2015/849.

The regulatory intent of Article 5 is to ensure that third-country authorities are aware of potential risks and can take appropriate measures, without compromising the investigative integrity of the reporting entity or violating data protection principles. Consequently, the SAR transmitted to the third country must be a distinct document indicating that a report has been filed and sent to the local authorities of that third country. It is not required to include the substantive evidence or the raw data that triggered the filing. This distinction preserves the confidentiality of the reporting process while fulfilling the transparency obligations regarding the existence of the report.

Furthermore, the EBA and ESMA guidelines emphasize that the sharing of underlying data with third countries should only occur if explicitly authorized by the competent authority of the Member State or if required by specific international cooperation agreements that provide adequate safeguards. In the absence of such specific authorization, the default position is the transmission of the SAR notification alone. This approach balances the need for international cooperation in combating financial crime with the imperative to protect sensitive financial data and maintain the effectiveness of the reporting mechanism. Therefore, the requirement refers solely to the notification of the SAR's existence and filing status, not the underlying data itself.

question:
According to the amended validation rule column 060, row 010
of template C 05.01
should be reported as greater or equal to zero.
On the other hand, the ITS sign convention states any amount that increases the own funds or the capital requirements shall be reported as a positive figure while any amount that reduces the total own funds or the capital requirements shall be reported as a negative figure.
In our example given in ‘Background on the question’ box, row 010, column 060 (Total adjustments) represents net deductions and therefore is to be reported as negative. In fact in EBA Q&A
2015_2482
it states that those rows of column 060 which show deductions according to final provisions are reported with a negative sign.
ground_truth:
The amended validation rule v3693_s expects {r010, c060} of template C 05.01 of Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 (ITS on Supervisory Reporting) to be reported as a positive value. This is incorrect, as this cell represents a sum of capital items and instruments (reported with a positive sign in accordance with the COREP sign convention), deductions (reported with a negative sign) and other elements, which can turn both positive and negative.
The scope of application of v3693_s will be adjusted to exclude {C 05.01, r010, c060}.

meta.subject_matter: Amended validation rule v3693_s in v2.6

baseline.text: The requirement for reporting the value in column 060, row 010 of template C 05.01 is governed by the specific validation logic embedded within the template's technical specifications rather than the general sign convention of the ITS. While the ITS sign convention dictates that amounts increasing own funds or capital requirements are positive and those reducing them are negative, this principle applies to the underlying data fields (e.g., column 060, row 001) before aggregation. Column 060, row 010, labeled "Total adjustments," represents a net figure derived from the sum of positive and negative adjustments reported in preceding rows. Consequently, the validation rule v3693_s in version 2.6 explicitly mandates that this net total must be greater than or equal to zero. This constraint ensures that the template captures only net deductions or zero, effectively filtering out scenarios where net adjustments are positive. The EBA's guidance in Q&A 2015_2482 confirms that rows within column 060 showing deductions according to final provisions are reported with a negative sign; however, the "Total adjustments" row aggregates these individual signed figures. If the sum of these signed adjustments results in a net deduction, the value is negative; if it results in a net increase, the value is positive. The validation rule's "greater than or equal to zero" constraint implies that the reporting framework for this specific row is designed to capture only net deductions or null values, thereby precluding the reporting of net positive adjustments in this specific line item. Therefore, while the individual components follow the ITS sign convention, the aggregated total in row 010 is subject to the stricter validation logic defined in the template's technical standards, which restricts the reported value to non-negative figures representing net deductions.

question: Does Article 412(5) of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR) prohibit the competent authorities from imposing a “Liquidity-Add-on” (e.g. LCR-requirement above 100%; similarly to a Capital-Add-on according to Article 104(2) of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD) according to Article 104(1)(k) and/or Article 105?
ground_truth:
Article 412(5) of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR) states that "Member States may maintain or introduce national provisions in the area of liquidity requirements before binding minimum standards for liquidity coverage requirements are specified and fully introduced in the Union in accordance with Article 460. Member States or competent authorities may require domestically authorised institutions, or a subset of those institutions, to maintain a higher liquidity coverage requirement up to 100% until the binding minimum standard is fully introduced at a rate of 100% in accordance with Article 460." Thus, Article 412 states the possibility of having national liquidity provisions during the phase where the LCR is being specified and implemented, i.e. until 1 January 2018.
Article 104(1)(k) and Article 105 of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD) refer to the supervisory powers with respect to imposing "specific liquidity requirements, including restrictions on maturity mismatches between assets and liabilities" (Article 104(1)(k)) and the assessment by competent authorities of "whether any imposition of a specific liquidity requirement is necessary to capture liquidity risks to which an institution is or might be exposed" (Article 105). These paragraphs refer to the supervisory evaluation process of institutions' liquidity, i.e. Pillar II. Under the specific framework of Article 105 of the CRD, competent authorities can impose additional liquidity requirements if deemed relevant for a specific institution or, also, for institutions with similar risk profiles according to Article
103
97(4a)
of Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD). An example of such additional requirement could be an LCR above 100%, but other metrics may apply as well depending on the specific institution's liquidity and funding profile.
In addition, Article 458 of the CRR allows for the relevant competent or designated authority to set additional liquidity requirements for domestically authorised institutions, or a subset of those institutions, as a means of addressing macro-prudential or systemic risk identified at the level of the Member State with the potential to have serious negative consequences to the financial system and the real economy in a specific Member State.

meta.subject_matter: Supervisory powers Liquidity

baseline.text:
Article 412(5) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) does not prohibit competent authorities from imposing a "Liquidity-Add-on" such as a Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement exceeding 100%. The provision explicitly states that the requirements set out in Articles 412(1) and (2) shall not apply to credit institutions or investment firms that are subject to a higher LCR requirement imposed by the competent authority. This language confirms that the 100% baseline is a minimum floor rather than a strict ceiling, thereby legally validating the imposition of additional buffers. The legislative intent of Article 412(5) is to ensure that the CRR framework remains flexible and does not preclude national supervisors from applying stricter standards where necessary to address specific liquidity risks or macro-prudential concerns. This mechanism mirrors the approach found in the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD IV), where Article 104(2) explicitly allows for a "Capital-Add-on" above the minimum capital requirements. Consequently, the supervisory powers granted to competent authorities under Article 412(5) are fully compatible with, and indeed necessary for, the implementation of a Liquidity-Add-on. Such measures are consistent with the broader objective of the CRR to ensure the resilience of the financial system, as reinforced by the EBA's technical standards which emphasize the need for proportionate and risk-sensitive supervisory interventions. Therefore, a competent authority may lawfully mandate an LCR of 110% or higher for specific institutions without violating the provisions of Article 412(5) of the CRR.

[Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, Article 412(5)]

question: A clarification regarding the scope of application for forbearance of Non-performing Exposures is required.
ground_truth: In case forbearance measures do not result in an improvement in the situation of the debtor but in liquidation, termination or insolvency procedure, the exposure to which forbearance measures is related shall be classified as non-performing forborne exposure and reported as such in FINREP. Indeed, the liquidation, termination or insolvency procedure can be considered as a default event in application of Article 178(3) (e) and (f) of Regulation (EU) 575/2013 (CRR), and even if it were not identified as a default event, it evidences a concern regarding the full repayment of the exposure according to the post-forbearance conditions.

meta.subject_matter: Forbearance of Non-performing Exposures

baseline.text:
The scope of application for forbearance of Non-performing Exposures (NPEs) within the context of FINREP reporting is strictly defined by Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) and its implementing technical standards. Specifically, Article 100(1) of CRR establishes the fundamental requirement that credit institutions must report all exposures classified as non-performing. However, the treatment of exposures subject to forbearance measures requires precise alignment with the definitions provided in the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/1032, which sets out the technical standards for the application of CRR.

According to Article 2(1)(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/1032, an exposure is considered non-performing if it is either past due by more than 90 days or classified as non-performing by the credit institution. Crucially, Article 2(1)(2) clarifies that this classification applies regardless of whether the exposure is subject to a forbearance agreement, provided the exposure meets the criteria for non-performance. Consequently, forbearance measures do not automatically exclude an exposure from the NPE category; rather, they are a specific type of risk mitigation measure that must be disclosed alongside the underlying non-performing status.

In the context of FINREP reporting, Article 100(1) of CRR mandates the inclusion of all such exposures in the relevant tables, specifically Table 100.1 and Table 100.2, which detail the composition of non-performing exposures. The supervisory reporting guidelines further require that the nature of the forbearance measure be explicitly identified to ensure transparency. Therefore, credit institutions must report NPEs subject to forbearance as non-performing exposures, while simultaneously providing detailed information regarding the specific forbearance terms and the credit institution's assessment of the exposure's recoverability. This ensures that the supervisory authorities receive a complete and accurate picture of the credit institution's asset quality, distinguishing between the status of the exposure and the specific contractual arrangements in place to manage it.

question: What exposure value have to be taken into consideration to verify threshold of 10% of total exposures in all exposures classes according to Article 5 (a) (4)? Should the total exposures be taken as reported in row 010 column 010 of template 7 of Annex I as original exposure pre conversion factors? Which institutions should report information on the geographical distribution of exposures by country on template CR GB 1, CR GB 2? Should only those institutions report CR GB 1, CR GB 2 templates whose ‘non-domestic’ exposures are equal or higher than 10% of total exposures?
ground_truth: As clarified with the reference to rows 850 and 860 of C 04.00 Template in Annex I of the Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 13 ITS on Supervisory Reporting of institutions (ITS), the value used to calculate the threshold of Article 5(a)(4) of the ITS is the original exposure pre conversion factors. For exposures, the risk weighted assets of which are calculated under the Standardised Approach in Chapter 2 of Part 3, Title II of Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013 (CRR), the values relevant for the threshold would correlate to the values reported in {C 07.00, r010, c010} of Annex I of the ITS. For exposures, the risk weighted assets of which are calculated under the IRB Approach in Chapter 3 of Part 3, Title II of CRR the values relevant for the threshold would correlate to the values reported in {C 08.01, r010, c020} of Annex I of the ITS. According to the threshold of Article 5(a)(4) of the ITS, only those institutions whose ratio of non-domestic original exposures pre conversion factors to total original exposures pre conversion factors are equal or higher than 10% shall report templates C 09.01 and C 09.02. The entry and exit criteria of Article 4 of the ITS should be considered.

meta.subject_matter: ITS on supervisory reporting under the CRR COREP CR GB template

baseline.text:
Institutions must determine the exposure value by applying the conversion factors specified in Article 429(1) of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) to the gross exposures reported in row 010, column 010 of template 7 of Annex I to the CRR. This calculation yields the "total exposures" required to verify the threshold of 10% of total exposures across all exposure classes under Article 5(a)(4) of the CRR. The verification process relies on these converted figures rather than the unadjusted original exposures, ensuring that the risk-weighted assessment aligns with the prudential standards set out in the regulation. Consequently, the threshold is calculated using the sum of exposures after the application of the relevant conversion factors, which may differ from the raw data submitted in the initial reporting line.

Regarding the geographical distribution of exposures, institutions are required to report data on the distribution of exposures by country on templates CR GB 1 and CR GB 2. However, this reporting obligation is conditional upon the institution's exposure profile. Specifically, only institutions whose 'non-domestic' exposures are equal to or higher than 10% of their total exposures (calculated as defined above) are mandated to submit information on the geographical distribution of exposures by country. This requirement ensures that supervisory resources are focused on institutions with significant cross-border risk profiles, as stipulated in the technical standards and guidance issued by the European Banking Authority and the European Securities and Markets Authority. Institutions failing to meet the 10% non-domestic exposure threshold are exempt from the detailed country-level breakdown, although they must still report their total exposure figures in the standard templates. This targeted approach facilitates efficient supervision while maintaining comprehensive oversight of significant cross-border banking activities within the European Union.

dpo.text:
Institutions must determine the exposure value for verifying the 10% threshold under Article 5(a)(4) of the CRR by aggregating exposures across all classes, excluding those already reported in the specific template. The total exposures to be considered for this threshold calculation are the original exposures reported in row 010, column 010 of template 7 of Annex I to the CRR, prior to the application of any conversion factors. This ensures that the threshold is applied to the gross exposure base before risk-weighting adjustments. Consequently, the 10% threshold applies to the sum of these original exposures across all classes, not to the risk-weighted amounts or post-conversion figures.

Regarding the geographical distribution of exposures, institutions are required to report data on the distribution by country on templates CR GB 1 and CR GB 2. However, this reporting obligation is conditional. Only institutions whose 'non-domestic' exposures are equal to or higher than 10% of their total exposures are mandated to complete and submit these templates. Institutions falling below this 10% threshold for non-domestic exposures are exempt from the reporting requirement for these specific templates. This conditional reporting mechanism is designed to ensure that supervisory resources are focused on institutions with significant cross-border exposure profiles. The threshold calculation itself relies on the total exposure base defined in the referenced row of template 7, ensuring consistency between the threshold verification and the subsequent geographical breakdown reporting. Therefore, the determination of the 10% threshold and the obligation to report geographical data are intrinsically linked to the original exposure figures in template 7 and the specific non-domestic exposure ratio of the institution.

question: Is validation rule v4787  correct?
ground_truth:
Paragraphs 80 and 81 of Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 (ITS on Supervisory reporting) clarify, that CRM techniques with substitution effects change the allocation of an exposure to a country in template C09.01 and C09.02 of Annex I of ITS on Supervisory Reporting only for data regarding “exposure value” (column 105 of C09.02) and “risk weighted exposure amount” (column 110 of C09.02).
In template C09.02, columns 020 to 070 include information on different aspects of exposures reported in column 010 “original exposure pre conversion factors”. Column 010 has the same definition as column 020 of template C08.01 of Annex I of ITS of Supervisory Reporting). While columns 030 and 050-060 refer directly to the exposures reported in column 010, the values reported in columns 040 and 070 only refer to those exposures of column 030 which newly defaulted according to the criteria of Article 178 of Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) during the 3-months period since the last reporting reference date.
Therefore, and in line with paragraph 81, data reported in column 070 shall be reported referring to the country of residence of the immediate obligor, i.e. without consideration of CRM techniques with substitution effects. Also, due to its common concept to newly defaulted exposures, column 070 will only include values if column 040 is reported.
Therefore v4787_m is correct.

meta.subject_matter: Validation Rule on C 09.02 Template - V4787

baseline.text: Validation rule V4787 for template C 09.02 is correct as it accurately enforces the data quality requirements mandated by the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR) regarding the calculation of IP losses. Specifically, the rule ensures that the sum of the individual IP loss components reported in the template aligns with the total IP loss figure derived from the underlying asset-level data, thereby preventing aggregation errors that could distort the bank's risk-weighted asset calculations. This validation is critical because C 09.02 serves as the primary source for determining the impairment provisions under the expected credit loss (ECL) framework, and any discrepancy here would directly impact the prudential capital requirements. The rule operates by cross-checking the reported values against the mathematical consistency of the input fields, ensuring that the sum of the gross impairment, the allowance for expected losses, and the recoverable amount equals the total IP loss as defined in the regulatory technical standards. Furthermore, the validation logic adheres to the EBA's guidance on supervisory reporting, which emphasizes the necessity of automated checks to detect inconsistencies before data submission to the European Central Bank. By mandating this specific validation, the regulation aims to enhance the reliability of the consolidated financial reporting system, ensuring that supervisors receive accurate and consistent data for the assessment of the banking sector's resilience. Consequently, any submission failing this validation must be corrected to reflect the true economic reality of the bank's credit portfolio, in full compliance with the integrity standards set forth in the CRR and its implementing acts.

The rule operates by cross-checking the reported values against the mathematical consistency of the input fields, ensuring that no negative IP losses are reported where positive values are expected, and that the total does not exceed the sum of its parts. This approach adheres to the EBA's Technical Standards on Supervisory Reporting, which require that all templates must include validation rules to ensure data integrity and comparability across the EU financial sector. Furthermore, the rule reflects the specific methodology outlined in the EBA's Guidelines on the calculation of IP losses, which dictate that these losses must be calculated based on the expected loss component of the impairment allowance. By enforcing these constraints, V4787 facilitates the accurate transmission of high-quality data to the European Central Bank and national competent authorities, ensuring that the supervisory framework remains robust against potential manipulation or clerical errors in the reporting of impaired assets.

question: In template F18.00 rows 211 to 231 for columns 120 and 140 and in template F19.00 rows 211 to 231 for columns 100 and 130 need to be opened. Validation rules v6012_m, v6013_m and v6014_m need to be deactivated as long as these positions are greyed out. These VRs may not be applicable for reporters under nGAAP that measure debt instruments at strict LOCOM and recognize accumulated impairment for performing exposures. Furthermore debt instruments measured at strict LOCOM under Austrian nGAAP are recognized as impaired assets in case there are negative credit-risk induced value adjustments.
ground_truth:
In ANNEX IV to Regulation (EU) No 680/2014 (ITS on Supervisory Reporting)
the following cells which are currently greyed out will be opened:
columns c140 and c120 in template 18.00 for rows r211 to r231 and
columns c100 and c130 in template 19.00 for rows r211 to r231.
VRs v6012_m, v6013_m and v6014_m were deactivated on 10 March 2021 and will be changed in order to take account of the values in row 231.

meta.subject_matter: IFRS 9, validation rules v6012_m, v6013_m and v6014_m

baseline.text: The deactivation of validation rules v6012_m, v6013_m, and v6014_m for the specified template cells is a necessary technical adjustment to accommodate the specific accounting treatments permitted under national GAAPs, particularly Austrian nGAAP, which diverge from the strict IFRS 9 impairment requirements. Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (CRR) establishes the framework for supervisory reporting but defers to national authorities regarding the precise application of accounting standards where permitted by the Single Rulebook. Specifically, Article 10(1) of CRR allows Member States to adopt national GAAPs for the measurement of financial assets, provided they do not contravene the fundamental principles of the Regulation. In the context of Austrian nGAAP, debt instruments measured at strict LOCOM may be recognized as impaired assets solely due to negative credit-risk induced value adjustments, even in the absence of a formal credit rating downgrade or significant probability of default indicative of IFRS 9 criteria. Consequently, the standard validation logic embedded in rules v6012_m through v6014_m, which enforces IFRS 9-based impairment thresholds, would incorrectly flag these legitimate Austrian disclosures as errors. The EBA's technical standards for FINREP reporting explicitly recognize the need for flexibility in validation rules to prevent the rejection of valid submissions from jurisdictions with divergent accounting practices. Therefore, when these specific rows are greyed out, indicating that the data is not subject to the standard IFRS 9 validation logic, the corresponding validation rules must be deactivated to ensure the integrity of the reporting process without imposing non-compliant IFRS 9 constraints on entities adhering to their national GAAP provisions. This approach aligns with the EBA's guidance on ensuring that supervisory reporting systems are robust yet adaptable to the diverse regulatory environments within the EU.

dpo.text:
The European Banking Authority (EBA) has issued specific guidance regarding the implementation of IFRS 9 impairment requirements within the Financial Reporting (FINREP) templates, particularly concerning the interaction between IFRS 9 and national accounting standards (nGAAP). For reporting entities operating under nGAAP frameworks, such as Austria's nGAAP, the treatment of debt instruments measured at strict Loan Commitment (LOCOM) differs from the standard IFRS 9 expected credit loss (ECL) model. Under Austrian nGAAP, debt instruments measured at strict LOCOM are recognized as impaired assets specifically when negative credit-risk induced value adjustments occur, rather than solely based on the probability of default thresholds inherent in the IFRS 9 three-stage model. Consequently, the validation rules v6012_m, v6013_m, and v6014_m, which enforce IFRS 9-specific logic for impairment stages and exposure classifications, may not be applicable to these specific exposures.

To ensure data integrity and prevent erroneous validation failures for entities reporting under such regimes, the EBA mandates that in template F18.00, rows 211 to 231 for columns 120 and 140, and in template F19.00, rows 211 to 231 for columns 100 and 130, the corresponding fields must be opened. Simultaneously, the aforementioned validation rules must be deactivated while these positions remain greyed out. This approach aligns with the principle that supervisory reporting should reflect the actual accounting treatment applied by the institution. The EBA's technical standards and guidance documents clarify that where national standards diverge from IFRS 9 regarding the recognition of impairment for performing exposures, the reporting entity must exclude the conflicting validation logic to avoid rejecting valid data submissions. This ensures that the FINREP data accurately represents the financial position of the institution without imposing IFRS 9 constraints on exposures governed by distinct nGAAP rules.
